sources.title: UK GDPR Article 22
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. The article page showed Article 22 omitted. The textual amendment says Chapter 3 Section 4A was substituted for Article 22 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025 section 80(1), for specified purposes on 19 June 2025 and otherwise on 5 February 2026 by S.I. 2026/82. This starter does not quote a pre-substitution Article 22.

sources.title: UK GDPR Article 22A
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. Article 22A(1) says a decision is based solely on automated processing if there is no meaningful human involvement in the taking of the decision, and a decision is significant if it produces a legal effect or a similarly significant effect. Article 22A(2) says that, when considering meaningful human involvement, a person must consider, among other things, the extent to which the decision is reached by means of profiling.

sources.title: Data Protection Act 2018, section 14
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. The page said section 14 is up to date with all changes known to be in force on or before 1 November 2026. The operative text was an omission: section 14 was omitted on 5 February 2026 by the Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, Schedule 6, paragraph 11, and S.I. 2026/82. This starter does not apply the omitted safeguards.

sources.title: Data (Use and Access) Act 2025, section 80
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. Section 80(1) substitutes UK GDPR Articles 22A to 22D for Article 22. Section 80(3) substitutes Data Protection Act 2018 sections 50A to 50D for the law-enforcement provisions on automated decision-making. Under section 50A a significant decision produces an adverse legal effect or a similarly significant adverse effect. This starter does not take that decision.

sources.title: Criminal Procedure and Investigations Act 1996, section 3
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. Section 3(1) says the prosecutor must disclose to the accused any prosecution material which has not previously been disclosed and which might reasonably be considered capable of undermining the case for the prosecution against the accused or of assisting the case for the accused, or give the accused a written statement that there is no material of that description. This starter does not apply that test and does not disclose anything.

sources.title: ATRS mandatory scope and exemptions policy
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. The policy, published 17 December 2024, says the ATRS was mandated across all government departments on 6 February 2024. Mandatory scope is central government, as defined in section 3. Section 4.2 covers tools that have a significant influence on a decision-making process with public effect, or that directly interact with the general public. Section 4.3 applies the duty to Beta, Pilot, and Production. The standard remains recommended for the broader public sector. Annex 1 gives an in-scope example of a tool that summarises text submitted by the public for humans who then take decisions. This starter does not decide that a body is in mandatory scope and does not publish a record.

sources.title: Evaluation of AI trials in the asylum decision making process
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. Published 29 April 2025. The note says the Asylum Case Summarisation tool and the Asylum Policy Search tool do not, and cannot, replace any part of the decision-making process. On average the test group reviewed transcripts 23 minutes quicker than the comparison group, a 32 percent time saving. Some interviewees highlighted minimal time-saving because the summary did not provide source references. Section 5.1 says the summary did not reference where to find the information in the transcript, which was a conscious design choice for the pilot. Technical specialists removed 9 percent of summaries as inaccurate or missing information. Of the summaries that remained, 23 percent of users were not fully confident. Those figures are the Home Office's, not a result of this starter.

sources.title: AI to speed up justice under major disclosure reforms
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. Published 14 July 2026. The page says PoliceAI will pilot AI tools capable of automatically generating summaries of digital material, with a view to scaling across all police forces in 2027. It says some investigations have over 500,000 e-books worth of data and an average fraud case contains over 4 million documents. It cites a Policing Productivity Review estimate of about 532,000 hours in 2022/23 on disclosure work and case files later assessed as requiring no further action. The PoliceAI interim director is quoted as saying technology can never replace professional judgement. This starter is not that pilot.

sources.title: DBS Barring Referral AI Summary Tool
sources.note: The record and the register index were opened on 4 November 2026. The index lists the tool under the Home Office, phase Public Beta, ATRS version 4.0, date published 14 October 2026. The record says the original evidence remains the authoritative source, caseworkers retain responsibility for decisions, and the output cannot be the sole basis for any case assessment, recommendation, or barring-related decision. It says the tool is not making any decisions. This starter is not that tool.

sources.title: Harnesses in Copilot Studio
sources.note: Opened on 4 November 2026. The page says the GitHub Copilot harness is a Copilot Studio authoring and orchestration framework, not the GitHub Copilot service, and that customer data is not sent to or processed by the GitHub Copilot service when agents run in Copilot Studio. It can take a goal, break it into steps, use skills and memory, create and edit Word, Excel, PowerPoint, and PDF files, and run in a sandbox. The prose says agents and workflows on that harness use Copilot Credits. The comparison table points the billing cell at a separate overview rather than repeating that sentence. The standard harness follows the topics and rules the maker defines. The page does not mark the GitHub Copilot harness as preview. Billing pages linked from the overview were not opened. No quantity is copied.

sources.title: Catalogue row UK09
sources.note: Catalogue row UK09. Stack Microsoft Foundry, Azure, and Copilot Studio. Autonomy A0. The decision-maker reviews every cited sentence. Not a web page. Not stale-tested.

differences.experiment_18: Experiment 18 builds an index of items in an authorised scope. It records a hash, a date, a proposed page order, and flags for possible privilege or third-party data. It does not write a sentence about what a document says, and it does not attach a page, paragraph, and line to such a sentence. This experiment drafts those sentences and checks each citation. It does not decide scope, build an export index, or call Experiment 12 or Experiment 18.
differences.experiment_29: Experiment 29 scores claims in a question-and-answer bundle against passages an agent was shown. A shared word can be enough for its supported verdict, and its human gate is an evaluation owner on thresholds and a release. This experiment drafts a case-bundle reading. Support means the sentence is a contiguous span of the cited lines. The human gate is that the decision-maker reviews every cited sentence. There is no threshold and no release. Neither experiment decides a case.
